description: Musa acuminata: a giant herb whose 'trunk' is a pseudostem of leaf sheaths.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.description: A fungal rot of ripening banana fruit, mostly after harvest.
diseases.causes: Spores from dead leaves and flower remains infect green fruit through wounds; the rot appears as the fruit ripens.
symptoms: Dark brown to black, sunken spots on ripening fruit
Salmon-pink spore masses on the spots
Spots join; the rot reaches the pulp
diseases.effect: Fruit spoils quickly in ripening and storage.
diseases.untreated: Losses rise with bruising and warm storage.

steps.title: Remove dead leaves and flower remains near the bunch
steps.instruction: Pick off dead leaves and flower remains near the bunch when the plants are dry and take them away.

steps.title: Handle fruit gently
steps.instruction: Avoid bruising at harvest and packing.

steps.title: Cool and clean the packing area
steps.instruction: Wash and cool fruit soon after harvest.

prevention.title: Remove dead leaves and flower parts
Bag bunches
prevention.detail: Protects fruit from spores and bruising.

lifecycle: Spores live on dead leaves and flower parts.
They infect green fruit, often at wounds.
The infection waits until ripening.
Black, sunken spots spread over the fruit.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: banana anthracnose

diseases.name: Black Leaf Streak (Black Sigatoka)
diseases.description: The most damaging leaf disease of banana: streaks that merge and kill large areas of leaf.
diseases.causes: Wind and rain spread spores from infected leaves; frequent rain and high humidity favour it.
symptoms: Small red-brown streaks parallel to the leaf veins
Streaks widen into dark brown to black spots with grey centres
Spots merge and large areas of leaf die
diseases.effect: Plants lose leaves before the bunch fills; fruit is small and ripens early.
diseases.untreated: Yield losses of 30-50% or more where it is not controlled.

steps.title: Cut off badly affected leaves
steps.instruction: Remove leaves or leaf parts with dead areas and put them on the ground face down.

steps.title: Improve drainage and spacing
steps.instruction: Drain wet spots and remove excess suckers.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide on the local programme on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

lifecycle: Spores come from infected leaves.
Wind and rain carry them to young leaves.
Red-brown streaks form along the veins.
Streaks merge and kill the leaf.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: banana black leaf streak
Content: general plant-pathology knowledge (APS disease compendia, university extension guides, UC IPM); not reviewed by a plant pathologist.

diseases.name: Banana Bunchy Top
diseases.pathogen: Banana bunchy top virus (BBTV, a babuvirus)
diseases.description: A virus disease that stunts banana plants into a bunched rosette of narrow, upright leaves.
diseases.causes: The banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa) carries the virus; infected suckers and planting material carry it farther.
symptoms: Dark green dots and dashes ('Morse code') along the leaf veins and midrib
New leaves narrow, short, upright and bunched at the top
Yellow, wavy leaf margins; no bunch, or a small one
diseases.effect: Infected plants produce little or no fruit.
diseases.untreated: Without removal, the virus spreads through the plantation.

steps.title: Report and confirm
steps.instruction: Check whether bunchy top must be reported in your area.
steps.rationale: It is a regulated disease in many places.

steps.title: Destroy infected plants and their suckers
steps.instruction: Kill the aphids on the plant first, then dig out the whole mat.

lifecycle: Banana aphids feed on an infected plant.
They carry the virus to healthy plants.
Dark green dashes appear along the veins.
New leaves bunch at the top; no fruit forms.
conditions: Infected plants left in the field.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: banana bunchy top
Content: general plant-pathology knowledge (APS disease compendia, university extension guides, UC IPM); not reviewed by a plant pathologist.

diseases.name: Cigar End Rot
diseases.description: A fungal rot that turns the flower end of banana fingers dry and ashen, like the burnt end of a cigar.
diseases.causes: Spores infect the dying flower parts at the finger tips in wet weather, and the rot spreads into the fruit.
symptoms: Dark, dry rot at the tip of the finger
Grey-white powdery fungus on the rotted end, like cigar ash
The rot spreads slowly back along the finger
diseases.untreated: Many fingers of a bunch can be affected in wet seasons.

steps.title: Remove flower remains
steps.instruction: Take off the dead flower parts from young fingers.

steps.title: Bag the bunches
steps.instruction: Cover young bunches with plastic sleeves.

steps.title: Remove the male bud
steps.instruction: Cut off the male bud after the last hand sets.

prevention.title: Remove dead leaves and flower parts

lifecycle: Spores land on dying flower parts.
They infect the tip of the finger.
A dry, dark rot forms at the tip.
Grey 'ash' spores form on the rot.
conditions: Flower parts left on the fingers.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: banana cigar end rot
Content: general plant-pathology knowledge (APS disease compendia, university extension guides, UC IPM); not reviewed by a plant pathologist.

diseases.name: Cordana Leaf Spot
diseases.description: A fungal leaf spot of banana with large, pale, oval spots ringed in yellow.
diseases.causes: Spores spread by wind and rain from infected leaves; it often follows other leaf diseases and wounds.
symptoms: Oval, pale brown spots with concentric zones
A dark border and a bright yellow halo round each spot
Spots often start at the leaf edge or along the midrib
diseases.effect: Reduces healthy leaf area; usually less damaging than Sigatoka.
diseases.untreated: Many spots combine with other diseases to kill leaves early.

steps.title: Remove badly spotted leaves
steps.instruction: Pick off badly spotted leaves when the plants are dry and take them away.

steps.title: Improve drainage and spacing
steps.instruction: Lower the humidity in the canopy.

steps.title: Protective spray
steps.instruction: Spray a registered fungicide if it spreads on the label's schedule.
steps.rationale: Protects healthy growth; it cannot cure what is already infected.

lifecycle: Spores come from infected leaves.
Wind and rain carry them to wet leaves.
Oval spots with yellow halos form.
Spots merge with other leaf damage.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: banana cordana leaf spot
Content: general plant-pathology knowledge (APS disease compendia, university extension guides, UC IPM); not reviewed by a plant pathologist.

diseases.name: Panama Disease (Fusarium Wilt)
diseases.pathogen: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (incl. Tropical Race 4)
diseases.description: A soil-borne fungal wilt that blocks the water vessels of banana plants; Tropical Race 4 also kills Cavendish.
diseases.causes: The fungus lives in the soil for decades and enters through the roots; it spreads in soil on boots, tools, vehicles, water and infected planting material.
symptoms: Older leaves yellow from the margins inward
Leaves collapse at the petiole and hang down round the pseudostem like a skirt
Brown to red-brown streaks inside the pseudostem
diseases.effect: Infected plants die without a bunch.
diseases.untreated: The soil stays infested for decades; the disease spreads field to field.

steps.title: Report and quarantine the spot
steps.instruction: Report suspected Panama disease and fence off the area.
steps.rationale: Tropical Race 4 is a quarantine disease in many countries.

steps.title: Destroy infected plants on site
steps.instruction: Kill and leave plants in place as advised; do not move soil or plant material.

steps.title: Disinfect boots and tools
steps.instruction: Use foot baths and clean tools and vehicles.

lifecycle: The fungus lives in the soil for decades.
It enters through the roots.
It blocks the water vessels.
Leaves yellow, collapse and the plant dies.
sources: PlantSeg (Wei et al. 2024, CC BY 4.0) class: banana panama disease
